summary: Defines the LDAP Client Update Protocol (LCUP), which lets an LDAP client stay synchronized with the contents of a directory tree held by a server and be notified when that content changes.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like subscribing to a phone book so that you get told whenever a name or number changes, rather than checking every page yourself.

questions: how to sync with an ldap directory
what is the ldap client update protocol
subtitle: How an LDAP client pulls a directory's changes, with a cookie that remembers where it left off.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients that keep a local copy of directory data, sync other data stores or react to changes had no single protocol that kept them up to date, online or off.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a Sync Request control to an LDAP search. The server returns entries with a Sync Update control, and a cookie that records how current the client is. The client sends that cookie next time.
tldr.outcome: The server keeps no per-client state, and the client decides when to pull changes. A server can answer lcupReloadRequired to force a full reload.

today: RFC 3928 is a Proposed Standard from October 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Goals and Design Principles
sections.content:
The LDAP Client Update Protocol (LCUP) lets an LDAP client synchronize with the content of a directory information tree (DIT) held by a server and be notified of changes. The RFC names three problem areas: mobile clients that keep a read-only local copy (for example a mail client with the corporate address book), applications that synchronize heterogeneous data stores such as a meta directory, and clients that must act when an entry changes, such as creating or deleting a mailbox when a person entry is added or removed.

Server-to-server synchronization is out of scope. The RFC points to the LDAP replication work called LDUP (RFC 3384) for that.

The server does not keep state for each client. The client stores how up to date it is, chooses when and from where to fetch changes, and starts every update session itself, so it "pulls" the changes. No LCUP-specific agreement between client and server is needed beforehand, and the server's access control policies still apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The library does not remember what each reader has seen. Every reader keeps their own bookmark and asks for news whenever they like.

sections.title: UUIDs, Schemes, Cookies and Contexts
sections.content:
Distinguished names can change, so entries are identified by a UUID, which MUST be used and is returned in the Sync Update control. Servers SHOULD also expose it as a single-valued operational attribute such as entryUUID and SHOULD allow efficient searches on it. A server also MUST support UUIDs.

The cookie holds the state of the client's data relative to the server's. Each cookie format is identified by a scheme, an object identifier that MUST be unique per scheme. A cookie may be opaque or may have a documented format, and the RFC expects exposed schemes to be documented in RFCs.

An LCUP Context is a part of the DIT enabled for LCUP. A server can support several, each with its own cookie scheme. A search does not cross a context boundary. It returns a SearchResultReference instead, and the client must follow it, keeping a mapping from each LDAP URL to its cookie.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry has a permanent ID badge, so you can find it even if it moves to a new desk. The cookie is your bookmark, and the scheme says what kind of bookmark it is.

sections.title: The Three Controls and Result Codes
sections.content:
LCUP defines three LDAP controls, with ASN.1 values encoded in BER. The Sync Request control (OID 1.3.6.1.1.7.1) goes on a searchRequest. Its updateType is syncOnly (0), syncAndPersist (1) or persistOnly (2). It may also carry sendCookieInterval, scheme and cookie.

The Sync Update control (1.3.6.1.1.7.2) rides on each SearchResultEntry and SearchResultReference. Its fields are stateUpdate, entryUUID, UUIDAttribute, entryLeftSet, persistPhase, scheme and cookie. entryUUID is optional in the syntax but MUST be used with SearchResultEntry.

The Sync Done control (1.3.6.1.1.7.3) rides on the SearchResultDone and carries an optional scheme and cookie.

Five new result codes, numbered 113 to 117, are defined, and implementations SHALL recognize them.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of stickers are used. One goes on your question, one on each answer, and one on the final goodbye note that carries your new bookmark.

sections.title: Running a Synchronization
sections.content:
For an initial synchronization or full resync, the client sets updateType to syncOnly or syncAndPersist and MUST NOT set a cookie. For an incremental sync, it MUST set both scheme and cookie, and SHOULD always use the latest cookie it received. A persistOnly request skips the sync phase, and any cookie sent with it is ignored.

A syncAndPersist search has two phases. In the sync phase the server sends what changed since the cookie. In the persist phase it keeps the search open and sends changes as they happen. The server MUST return an informational response right after the last sync entry, with persistPhase TRUE, so the client knows the persist phase has begun. It MUST NOT mix sync and persist entries.

An entry is returned as present if it is new to the result set or changed. It is returned as having left the set, with entryLeftSet TRUE, if it was deleted or moved or no longer matches. A change counts only if it touches an attribute the search requested. The server may report departures for entries the client never had, and the client MUST ignore those.

The server decides when the client is "in sync", since heavy update load could otherwise keep the sync phase from ever ending. It MAY send an entry more than once during sync, and the client SHOULD keep the last copy.
sections.plainLanguage: First you catch up on everything you missed. Then the library keeps the line open and tells you about each new change right away. A note says, now we are in the live part.

sections.title: Cookies, Termination and Resync
sections.content:
The server may return the cookie in any result. sendCookieInterval suggests how often, and the server SHOULD respect it. A client on a flaky wireless link might set it as low as 1. A client on limited bandwidth might set it high. The cookie is always returned in the Sync Done control on successful completion.

When finished, the server attaches a Sync Done control to the SearchResultDone. The cookie MUST be set if the result code is success or canceled. The server SHOULD also set it for lcupResourcesExhausted, timeLimitExceeded, sizeLimitExceeded or adminLimitExceeded. A client that wants its cookie sooner issues an LDAP Cancel operation (RFC 3909). The server then finishes with result code canceled and the cookie. If the client does not care, it can abandon the search or disconnect.

If the server cannot guarantee the client will converge, for example because its data was reloaded or the cookie is out of date, it SHOULD stop and return lcupReloadRequired. The client should then issue an initial synchronization request. For renames or deletes of whole subtrees, the server must either report every affected entry or force a resync.
sections.plainLanguage: When you finish, the library hands you a new bookmark. If your bookmark is too old to trust, it says to start over from page one.

sections.title: Client and Server Considerations
sections.content:
Clients should reuse a cookie only with the same search specification that produced it. Some servers allow a more restrictive one, a subset of the original results. If the base object is renamed, the client may find the new name by searching for the saved UUID. A persistent search needs an open TCP connection, so clients are encouraged to avoid persistent operations for non-essential tasks and to close idle connections.

If a client gets lcupResourcesExhausted or lcupSecurityViolation, it SHOULD wait at least 5 seconds before trying again, and exponential backoff is RECOMMENDED.

Servers should support several cookie schemes and send references first when the search crosses LCUP contexts. A replica update vector can serve as a cookie, but the RFC leaves cookie use across replicas undefined. The RFC also does not promise how fast changes are sent during the persist phase. Clients MUST set derefAliases to neverDerefAliases or derefFindingBaseObj, and servers return protocolError otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: If the library says it is too busy, wait a few seconds before asking again, and wait longer each time it says so.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Information about changes in a directory can be sensitive. Servers SHOULD be able to enforce access control on the entries returned, and MAY add access control over use of the LCUP controls.

A malicious client could open many persistent searches to use up server resources. Servers SHOULD be able to detect such clients and limit what a single client can consume. The protocol lets the server stop them by disconnecting, using lcupSecurityViolation or lcupResourcesExhausted.
sections.plainLanguage: The library should only tell each reader about the books they are allowed to see, and should show the door to anyone who asks for far too much.

sections.title: Features Left Out
sections.content:
The appendix lists ideas that were not included because they are hard for a server that keeps no client state. They include a per-entry change type (as in Triggered Search and Persistent Search), sending only changed attributes, client control of data size beyond the normal search sizeLimit, and ordering parents before children. The RFC says that sending only changes can leave a client with an incomplete entry, for example when a change moves an entry into the client's search scope.

The entryLeftSet flag is kept because the client otherwise cannot tell that an entry left the result set. The client may need a local index by DN or UUID to tell an added entry from a modified one.
sections.plainLanguage: Some extra features were skipped because they would make the library do too much bookkeeping. Whole entries are sent instead, so nothing is half-copied.
